client: Hey Luna, I’ve been really stressed lately about my grades. I got a disappointing grade on my last exam, and now I feel like I’m under so much pressure to maintain a perfect GPA. It’s just been weighing on me a lot. I know I should probably feel more confident, but I can’t shake this anxiety.
therapist: Hi there, I can really understand how stressful this must be for you. It’s natural to feel anxious when you’re facing academic pressures, and it sounds like you’re putting a lot of weight on yourself to maintain a perfect GPA. Can you tell me more about what thoughts are going through your mind when you think about your grades?

client: When I think about my grades, I feel like I’m constantly falling short of my own expectations. I worry that if I don’t get perfect grades, I won’t be able to get into the grad school I want, and that will affect my whole future. It’s like every grade feels like a make-or-break moment.
therapist: It sounds like you’re putting a lot of pressure on yourself, and that can be really tough. It’s understandable to worry about how your grades might impact your future, but it’s also important to consider whether these thoughts are helping or hindering you. What evidence do you have that one less-than-perfect grade will significantly impact your chances of getting into grad school?

client: I guess I don’t have concrete evidence that one bad grade will ruin everything, but it feels like it could. I’ve always been told that grad schools are so competitive, and I don’t want to take any chances. It’s hard to let go of that fear, even if I know it’s not entirely rational.
therapist: I can see how those fears can be really persistent, even when you know they might not be entirely rational. It’s tough to let go of them, especially when you’ve been told how competitive grad schools can be. Have you ever considered what steps you can take to manage this anxiety, or perhaps how you might reframe your thoughts to be more balanced?

client: I’ve tried to remind myself that one bad grade isn’t the end of the world, but it’s hard to fully believe it. I guess I could try to reframe my thoughts, but it feels like a big leap to go from feeling like I’m failing to feeling confident. It’s hard to shift that mindset when the stakes feel so high.
therapist: It’s completely understandable that it feels like a big leap to shift from feeling like you’re failing to feeling confident, especially when the stakes feel so high. It’s a gradual process, and it’s okay to take small steps. Maybe you could start by acknowledging the times when you’ve succeeded in the past, or by setting realistic goals for yourself. What are some small wins or successes that you can remind yourself of when you’re feeling this way?

client: I appreciate that suggestion, Luna. I do have some successes I can think of, like when I got a good grade on a tough project last semester. But it’s hard to remember those when I’m in the middle of feeling so anxious. I’ll try to make a list of my past successes, but I’m not sure how much it will help in the moment when I’m feeling overwhelmed.
therapist: It’s great that you’re willing to try making a list of your past successes—that can be a really helpful tool. It’s totally normal to have a hard time remembering those positive moments when you’re feeling anxious. One thing you might find useful is to keep that list handy, maybe even on your phone, so you can refer to it when you’re feeling overwhelmed. How do you think that might help you in the moment?

client: I think having that list on my phone could be helpful, but I’m still a bit skeptical about how much it will change how I feel in the moment. When I’m in the middle of feeling anxious, it can be hard to step back and look at things objectively, even with a list. I’ll try it though, and maybe it will make a difference over time.
therapist: I understand that you’re feeling a bit skeptical, and that’s completely normal. Change can take time, and it’s okay to have doubts. Having the list on hand might not instantly change how you feel, but it can be a helpful reminder of your capabilities and past successes, which can gradually build your confidence. How do you think you might use the list when you’re feeling overwhelmed, even if it’s just a small step?

client: I think I might try pulling up the list when I’m studying and start to feel really anxious. Even if it doesn’t completely alleviate the anxiety, maybe just seeing those successes will give me a little boost and help me keep going. It’s a small step, but I’ll give it a shot.
therapist: That’s a great plan, and I’m really glad you’re willing to give it a try. Even a small boost can make a big difference when you’re in the middle of a tough study session. Using the list as a quick reminder of your successes can help you stay motivated and keep things in perspective. How do you think you might also reward yourself for making progress, even if it’s just a small step forward?

client: I like the idea of rewarding myself for making progress. Maybe I could take a short break to do something I enjoy, like reading a chapter of a book or listening to some music, after I’ve made some progress on my studies. It might help me feel less overwhelmed and more motivated to keep going.
therapist: That’s a fantastic idea! Taking short breaks to do something you enjoy can be a great way to recharge and stay motivated. It’s all about balancing the pressure with self-care. How do you think you might build these breaks into your study routine, and what other small rewards might you consider as you make progress?

client: I think I can start by setting a timer for 45 minutes of focused study time, and then take a 10-minute break to do something I enjoy. It might feel a bit strange at first, but I can see how it could help me stay more focused and less anxious. Other small rewards could be treating myself to a favorite snack or a quick walk outside when I finish a particularly tough section of my studies. It’s a new approach, so I’m a bit nervous about how it will work, but I’m willing to give it a try.
therapist: That’s a really thoughtful plan, and I’m proud of you for setting it up. It’s completely normal to feel a bit nervous about trying a new approach, but breaking your study time into manageable chunks and rewarding yourself can make a big difference. How do you think you might adjust this plan if you find it’s not working as well as you hoped, or if you need to make it more flexible to fit your needs?

client: I think if it’s not working as well as I hoped, I might need to adjust the length of my study sessions or the type of rewards I give myself. Maybe I’ll start by trying it out for a week and see how it goes, and then make tweaks based on what I learn. It’s a bit daunting, but I’m open to making changes to find what works best for me.
therapist: It’s great to see you thinking so flexibly about how you can adapt your plan. Starting with a week to see how it goes is a smart approach, and being open to making changes based on what you learn is a key part of finding what works best for you. It’s completely normal to feel a bit daunted, but taking it one step at a time can really help. How do you think you might stay motivated during this trial period, especially if you encounter some challenges?
